description.narrative:
Regarding the enforcement of Public Financial Management (PFM) at the local level in key target areas of ANSA–Cambodia, a recent assessment on Civic Budget Awareness and Engagement was conducted to understand how women and youth (ages 15–35 and above) interact with their local government's budget processes. The study explores their awareness of public spending in key sectors such as education, infrastructure, and natural resources; examines their participation in community discussions; and identifies thebarriers that prevent them from engaging. The survey also assesses their interest in future participation and training, with the aim of understanding what support or resources would strengthen their involvement in monitoring public expenditure.
Since the commune/Sangkat elections in 2000, the Decentralization and De-concentration (D<(>&<)>D) reform has been implemented, establishing the elected Commune/SangkatCouncils. Principles of good governance were adopted, and commune/Sangkat administrations in Cambodia are required to apply participatory budgeting for local development through the Commune Investment Program (CIP), which forms part of the Commune Development Plan (CDP). This process encourages citizens to contribute ideas on development priorities within their communes and sangkats. Understanding how citizens—particularly youth and women—participate in planning and monitoring budgets is therefore critical for strengthening transparency, accountability, and local development outcomes.
This report summarizes findings from eight key informant interviews conducted across multiple communes and provinces, focusing on citizen engagement, budget allocation, and participatory mechanisms.The aim is to provide insights into current practices, identify challenges, and offer recommendations to enhance citizen participation. Drawing from field experiences, commune/Sangkat administrations continue to face major challenges related to civic participation and citizens’ understanding of local planning processes. Keychallenges include:
1) Local Budget Awareness and Direct Participation: Survey results reveal that while general awareness of local budgets is moderate, familiarity with specific expenditures remains low. Although 29.5% of respondents reported havingheard about the commune budget, a much larger share (70.5%) had either not heard about it or were unsure. Familiarity with spending in key sectors was consistently low, with average scores of 2.1 out of 5 for education and 2.4 for local infrastructure, indicating limited detailed knowledge.Despite this lack of awareness, a large majority (81.9%)believe that citizen participation in local budget planning is “very important” or “extremely important,” demonstrating a strong desire for involvement. However,actual participation remains limited. Only 47.7% of respondents—mostly youth engaged through ISAF and other social accountability initiatives—had attended a community meeting related to local budgeting, and only 36.4% had provided input on spending priorities. Even fewer (18.2%) reported participating in monitoring budget expenditures, such as verifying road repairs or school-related spending. This low engagement is further hindered by gaps in knowledge: 43.2% of respondents stated that they did not knowwhere or how to participate in budget discussions or monitoring.
2) Barriers to Engagement and Interest in Future Participation: The main barriers to civic participation revolve around limited access to information and fear of speaking up. Half of therespondents (50%) identified “lack of knowledge or access to information” as the primary obstacle, followed by “fear of speaking up or approaching the commune council” (27.3%). Other important barriers include the perception that budget matters are solely theresponsibility of local authorities (18.2%) and a general “culture of silence” (22.7%). These findings highlight that both institutional constraints and entrenched social norms contribute to low levels of civic engagement.Despite these barriers, interestinfuture engagement is strong. A significant majority (86.4%) expressed interest in learning more or receiving training on local budget processes and citizen monitoring. Topics most requested include “commune budget literacy” and “budget monitoringskills.”Additionally, 79.5% indicated willingness to join a community group focused on monitoring budget use, provided supportive conditions are met—such as receiving an official invitation from the commune and having meeting schedules shared via socialmedia.

participating-org.narrative: The Affiliated Network for Social Accountability (ANSA Cambodia) is a local non-profit and independent NGO that works to fight against corruption, promote human welfare, and protect citizen rights through the promotion of good governance. ANSA Cambodia initiates independent Social Accountability (SA) approaches while supplementing the existing public social accountability framework endorsed by the Royal Government of Cambodia. ANSA Cambodia still continues the valued mission and specifies the area of work in Cambodia and other related Lower Mekong Sub-region (LMS) country. As a multinational network with ANSA in East Asia and the Pacific (ANSA-EAP) and ANSA Global, we collectively define good governance as a way of decision-making and implementation of public development programs that aim to achieve desirable and beneficial results for both those who govern and those who are being governed. The key to good governance is the relationship between the government and its citizens, and their ability to constructively engage with each other. Social Accountability (SAc) is the concept and practice of this constructive engagement between citizens and their government; citizensmonitor the government’s use of public resources to improve service delivery, protect their rights, and promote community welfare. Beyond monitoring, ANSA enables citizens to voice their issues and concerns through coalition building and the use of communication and media. Through these methods, ANSA is able to influence public policy and improve public accountability. VISION: ANSA Cambodia envisions Cambodia developing into a country where citizens are capable and collaborative and a society with integrity, dignity and full of freedom in accordance to national and international laws. MISSION: ANSA Cambodia is to enhance citizen capacity, fight against corruption, and promote good governance to improve public service deliveries, public resources as well as natural resource management. ANSA Cambodia works with all policy and decision makers and stakeholders to benefit human rights, community welfare and povertyreduction. GOAL: ANSA Cambodia aims to make Cambodian citizens capable of building a society of good governance, integrity, democracy, human rights and better economy. CORE VALUE: Partnership, Resources, Innovation, Democracy and Equality (PRIDE)
